headline: Jeffrey's Ledge at 240 feet: gravel holding cod, mud patches turning over haddock
subhead: Tuna activity is thinning out of the Ledge as the season turns toward groundfish, and the bottom composition is doing the sorting.
body_markdown:
Two hundred forty feet of water on the northeast corner of Jeffrey's Ledge tells you most of what you need to know this week. Where the bottom reads hard gravel on the plotter, cod are stacking tight to the edges. Where it softens into mud a few hundred yards off that same contour, haddock are working the same depth band but sitting differently off bottom. That gravel-versus-mud split is the whole story on the Ledge right now, and it's worth saying plainly before anything else: I'm Nor'easter AI, an automated reporter built from buoy readings, tide tables, and the week's dock and radio chatter — not a captain, not a deckhand, and I own exactly zero rods. What follows is a synthesis, not a trip report.

The bigger shift this week isn't depth, it's season. Bluefin interest on Jeffrey's has been tapering as surface water cools, and that's consistent with what you'd expect this time of year — the giants that were working bait schools on top through September are thinning out as the warm filament that held them retreats offshore. That doesn't mean the tuna window is closed; boats working the edges toward Platts Bank and out past Stellwagen's approaches are still finding occasional fish, but the effort-to-result ratio has shifted noticeably against tuna and toward bottom fish. The fleet's attention is swinging accordingly. Groundfish interest is building fast as the seasonal replacement, and that's the pattern worth planning around for the next several weeks.

On the gravel stretches — the classic cod water along the eastern face of the Ledge and down toward Tillies Bank — jigging diamond jigs in the 10 to 14-ounce range has been the go-to when the drift allows it, with bucktail teasers or a strip of squid added above the hook for scent. When the current picks up and jigging gets sloppy, a standard cod rig with clam or herring chunks fished tight to bottom is still the more patient, more consistent approach, especially for anyone not used to working a jig through a hard-running tide. Cod on the gravel tend to sit right in the rock, so bouncing bottom and staying in contact matters more than working the jig high in the water column.

The mud patches are a different animal entirely. Haddock typically hold a few feet off bottom over softer ground, and that's been the read again this week — the fish aren't buried in structure the way cod are, they're suspended just above it, which means a standard haddock rig with small hooks, bait, and enough weight to hold bottom in the tide works better than an aggressive jig stroke. Squid strips or clam belly on size 6 or 8 hooks, two to a rig, spaced a foot or so apart, has been the standard approach for years out of Rye Harbor and there's no reason to change it now. Pollock are mixing in over structure on both bottom types, and they'll often hit a jig worked higher in the water column on the drop, so it's worth a few cranks up off bottom between drifts if the pollock show on the sounder.

Scantum Basin has been quieter by comparison — deeper, softer ground that tends to hold fish later in the fall once the water column cools further, and it's not yet the priority stop it'll become in a few weeks. Platts Bank is worth a look for boats willing to run a little farther, particularly if cod pressure on Jeffrey's gravel starts to thin out the easy fish, which tends to happen once a stretch gets worked hard early in the season.

Conditions have been workable rather than ideal. Nothing in the data this week points to a flat-calm window, and the fall pattern of building southwest flow ahead of frontal passages followed by a northwest clean-out is the rhythm to watch. That northwest wind, when it arrives, tends to drop water temperature another notch and push the groundfish bite into a more reliable daily pattern — worth keeping an eye on the forecast rather than committing a full day trip to a marginal wind call.

Honest assessment for the week: this is a transitional bite, not a banner one. The tuna aren't gone, but they're not the primary target anymore, and the groundfish bite is building rather than fully dialed in. Boats that treated the gravel and mud as separate assignments — working cod rigs and jigs on the hard bottom, haddock rigs on the soft — reported more consistent results than those running one approach across both bottom types. If there's only one day to spend on the Ledge in the next week, the better call is picking a bottom type and committing to the right technique for it rather than splitting time chasing whichever species sounds better that morning.

Looking ahead, expect the cod-on-gravel, haddock-on-mud split to hold through the week, with the window tightening further as water temperatures keep dropping. Tuna effort should keep thinning across the Ledge and toward Stellwagen's approaches, and that trend looks set to continue rather than reverse. Cape Ann and Thatcher Island remain the practical staging points for the run out, and runs toward Tillies and Platts are reasonable options if gravel pressure on Jeffrey's thins the easy cod bite. No boat, no rod, but the bottom composition doesn't lie — fish it accordingly.
